The Final
Series final. Eighty thousand people. Fireworks before the first ball. You call home from the tunnel.
The two suits are sitting on the bench, yes.
So are forty boys with bats. And Rocky. And the whole bus stand.
Nobody is drinking chai with anyone. Play.
The police took the two suits an hour ago. One of them cried.
Now hit something.
They bat first. 186 for 6 in the sixteenth over. The seventeenth begins. Karan is at mid-off. Every muscle in his face is still.
Ball three. A mistimed drive. It goes straight up. Straight down. Straight at the captain.
It hits his palms. It bounces out. The crowd groans. Karan doesn't look at the ball. He looks at the sky.
He takes it. Two hands, chest height, eyes closed. He holds the ball up to the stand where a seven-year-old is screaming.
202 to win. Seventeenth over of the chase. You're at the crease. Your phone is in the dressing room, buzzing on the bench. You know what it says.
Ball three. Short of a length. An easy single. Your partner calls. If you just... stop running...
Run. Play the ball on its merit.
Papa sells chai, not wickets.
Stop. Let them run you out.
Keep everyone safe. Throw away everything else.
You run like the stall is on fire. You make your ground by a bat's width. In the stands, Rathore lowers a phone, and nods.
Last over. Twelve to win.
12 off 6
The series final. Eighty thousand people. Twelve to win off Marco Venn. Nothing left to hide.
CHAMPIONS!
Rajgarh doesn't sleep tonight.
SO CLOSE
Eighty thousand people stand and clap anyway.
The last ball disappears over long-on. Vikrant reaches you first. Then Imran, somehow, from somewhere. Then the whole team, and Karan at the bottom of the pile, laughing like a boy.
Four runs short. You sink to your knees. A hand on your shoulder. Karan. "You ran, champ. That's the only thing anyone will remember."
You stop. The throw comes in. The bails come off. You walk back without looking at the replay screen. The crowd doesn't understand. Yet.
They lose by nine runs. In the dressing room, nobody talks to you. Kabir Sir doesn't look at you at all.
We have the texts. We have the numbers. They come back to a Mehra company, but not to Mehra. Not yet.
We need him to say it out loud. And tomorrow night he's presenting the awards. On stage. In front of everyone.
We had a wire on you, {first}. Or a phone. Or eighty thousand witnesses. It doesn't matter which.
I can't unsee what I saw at ball three.
Awards night. Raghav Mehra on stage. And you, in a suit, with a choice.
